\chapter{Communication Complexity — Lower Bound}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.DeterministicCC.FuncIndexing.LowerBound
\section{Overview}

This module proves the linear public-coin one-way lower bound of Kremer--Nisan--Ron for the
Index problem $\mathrm{IND}_n$ via Yao's distributional method, with fully explicit constants:
for $n \ge 300$, every public-coin one-way protocol for Index with error $1/9$ must
communicate more than $n/10$ bits.  The argument counts, for a deterministic one-way protocol,
the ``answer vectors'' $a(m) \in \{0,1\}^n$ realised by its messages, shows that most of
Alice's inputs are far (in Hamming distance) from every answer vector, and converts this into
a distributional error bound under the uniform distribution on pairs $(x,i)$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Answer vector of a message]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol}
For a deterministic one-way protocol $p$ for Index on $n$ bits and a message $m$ of $p$, the
\emph{answer vector} $a(m) \in \{0,1\}^n$ is the string whose $i$-th coordinate is Bob's output
$\mathrm{decode}(m, i)$ on receiving $m$ with index $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Answer set of a protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}
The \emph{answer set} $A$ of a one-way protocol $p$ is the finite set of all answer vectors
$a(m)$ as $m$ ranges over the messages of $p$, i.e.\ the image of the message type under
\texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bad input]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet}
Alice's input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ is \emph{bad} for the protocol $p$ if there is no answer vector
$a \in A$ with $d_H(x, a) < n/4$, where the radius $n/4$ is the real number (not its floor).
Equivalently, every realisable answer vector is at Hamming distance at least $n/4$ from $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Mismatch indices of an input]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
For a fixed input string $x$, the type of indices $i \in [n]$ on which the protocol $p$ errs,
i.e.\ the subtype $\{\, i : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \mid p.\mathrm{run}(x, i) \ne \mathrm{IND}_n(x, i) \,\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Incorrect input pairs]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
The type of input pairs $(x, i) \in \{0,1\}^n \times [n]$ on which the protocol $p$ is
incorrect, i.e.\ the subtype of pairs with $p.\mathrm{run}(x, i) \ne \mathrm{IND}_n(x, i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Incorrect pairs as a sigma type]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairEquivSigma}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairEquivSigma}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
The equivalence between the type of incorrect pairs $(x, i)$ of $p$ and the dependent sum
$\Sigma_{x \in \{0,1\}^n}\, \mathrm{mismatch}(p, x)$ of the per-input mismatch index types,
given by $((x, i), h) \mapsto (x, (i, h))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Mismatch count equals Hamming distance]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype_card_eq_hammingDist}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype_card_eq_hammingDist}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
For a fixed input string $x$, the number of indices $i$ on which $p$ errs equals the Hamming
distance between $x$ and the answer vector of Alice's message on $x$:
\[
  \abs{\mathrm{mismatch}(p, x)} = d_H\bigl(x,\ a(\mathrm{send}(x))\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Incorrect pairs counted by summing mismatches]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype_card_eq_sum}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype_card_eq_sum}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairEquivSigma, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
The number of incorrect input pairs $(x, i)$ of $p$ equals the sum, over all strings
$x \in \{0,1\}^n$, of the number of indices $i$ on which $p$ errs at $x$:
\[
  \abs{\mathrm{badPairs}(p)} = \sum_{x \in \{0,1\}^n} \abs{\mathrm{mismatch}(p, x)}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[At most $2^c$ answer vectors]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet_card_le_pow_cost}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet_card_le_pow_cost}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}
A one-way protocol $p$ of cost $c$ realises at most $2^c$ distinct answer vectors:
$\abs{A} \le 2^{p.\mathrm{cost}}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Bad inputs are far from their own answer vector]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput_implies_hammingDist_ge}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput_implies_hammingDist_ge}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput}
If $x$ is a bad input for $p$, then the Hamming distance from $x$ to the answer vector of its
own message satisfies $d_H\bigl(x, a(\mathrm{send}(x))\bigr) \ge n/4$ (as real numbers).
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Half bad inputs give error at least $1/8$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.distributionalError_ge_one_eighth_of_bad_half}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.distributionalError_ge_one_eighth_of_bad_half}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput_implies_hammingDist_ge, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype_card_eq_sum, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype_card_eq_hammingDist, CommunicationComplexity.uniformOn_univ_measureReal_eq_card_filter}
Let $p$ be a deterministic one-way protocol for $\mathrm{IND}_n$.  If at least $2^{n-1}$ of
Alice's $2^n$ inputs are bad for $p$ (no answer vector of $p$ lies within Hamming distance
$n/4$), then the distributional error of $p$ on $\mathrm{IND}_n$ under the uniform
distribution on pairs $(x, i)$ is at least $1/8$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Binomial coefficients grow by a factor $3$ below $n/4$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.choose_three_mul_le_succ_choose_quarter}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.choose_three_mul_le_succ_choose_quarter}
\leanok
For natural numbers $n, i$ with $i < \lfloor n/4 \rfloor$, one has
$3 \binom{n}{i} \le \binom{n}{i+1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Hamming ball of radius $\lfloor n/4 \rfloor$ has at most $2\binom{n}{\lfloor n/4\rfloor}$ points]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.hammingBall_card_quarter_le_two_mul_choose}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.hammingBall_card_quarter_le_two_mul_choose}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.choose_three_mul_le_succ_choose_quarter, CommunicationComplexity.ballVol_binary, CommunicationComplexity.hammingBall, CommunicationComplexity.hammingBall_card}
For every $n$ and every centre $a \in \{0,1\}^n$, the Hamming ball of radius
$\lfloor n/4 \rfloor$ around $a$ satisfies
\[
  \abs{B_{\lfloor n/4 \rfloor}(a)} \le 2 \binom{n}{\lfloor n/4 \rfloor}
\]
(as real numbers).
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Euler's number is at most $68/25$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.exp_one_le_68_div_25}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.exp_one_le_68_div_25}
\leanok
The real number $e = \exp(1)$ satisfies $e \le 68/25 = 2.72$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Ratio $n / \lfloor n/4 \rfloor$ is at most $101/25$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.div_nat_div_four_le_101_25}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.div_nat_div_four_le_101_25}
\leanok

For every natural number $n \ge 300$, the real ratio $n / \lfloor n/4 \rfloor$ is at most
$101/25 = 4.04$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Quarter binomial coefficient is at most $11^{\lfloor n/4 \rfloor}$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.choose_quarter_le_eleven_pow}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.choose_quarter_le_eleven_pow}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.div_nat_div_four_le_101_25, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.exp_one_le_68_div_25}
For every natural number $n \ge 300$,
\[
  \binom{n}{\lfloor n/4 \rfloor} \le 11^{\lfloor n/4 \rfloor}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Good inputs are covered by Hamming balls around answer vectors]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.goodInput_card_le}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.goodInput_card_le}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.hammingBall_card_quarter_le_two_mul_choose, CommunicationComplexity.hammingBall}
Let $\mathrm{good}$ be the set of inputs $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ that are not bad for $p$ (those
within Hamming distance $< n/4$ of some answer vector).  Then
\[
  \abs{\mathrm{good}} \le \abs{A} \cdot 2 \binom{n}{\lfloor n/4 \rfloor},
\]
where $A$ is the answer set of $p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Small cost forces at least half the inputs to be bad]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput_card_ge_half_of_small_cost}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput_card_ge_half_of_small_cost}
\leanok

If $n \ge 300$ and the deterministic one-way protocol $p$ for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ has cost at most
$\lfloor n/10 \rfloor$, then at least $2^{n-1}$ of the $2^n$ inputs $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ are bad
for $p$ (no answer vector of $p$ lies within Hamming distance $n/4$ of $x$).
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Cost at most $n/10$ forces error above $1/9$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.one_ninth_lt_distributionalError_of_cost_le}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.one_ninth_lt_distributionalError_of_cost_le}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput_card_ge_half_of_small_cost, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.distributionalError_ge_one_eighth_of_bad_half, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist}
For $n \ge 300$, every deterministic one-way protocol $p$ for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ with
$p.\mathrm{cost} \le \lfloor n/10 \rfloor$ has distributional error strictly greater than
$1/9$ under the uniform distribution on pairs $(x, i)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Distributional one-way lower-bound hypothesis for Index]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist}
For a real $\varepsilon$ and a natural number $c$, the proposition that every deterministic
one-way protocol $p$ for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ with $p.\mathrm{cost} \le c$ has distributional
error strictly greater than $\varepsilon$ under the uniform input distribution
\texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist}.  This is the hypothesis
of the easy direction of Yao's minimax principle for one-way protocols, specialised to Index.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Index satisfies the lower-bound hypothesis at $(1/9, n/10)$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound_one_ninth_of_large}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound_one_ninth_of_large}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.one_ninth_lt_distributionalError_of_cost_le}
For $n \ge 300$, the predicate
\texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound}
holds at error $\varepsilon = 1/9$ and cost budget $c = \lfloor n/10 \rfloor$: every
deterministic one-way protocol for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ of cost at most $\lfloor n/10 \rfloor$ has
uniform-distributional error greater than $1/9$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Distributional lower bound implies public-coin one-way lower bound]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_of_distributionalLowerBound}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_of_distributionalLowerBound}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.lt_communicationComplexity_of_forall_distributionalError_gt}
If every deterministic one-way protocol for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ of cost at most $c$ has
uniform-distributional error greater than $\varepsilon$, then the public-coin one-way
communication complexity of $\mathrm{IND}_n$ at error $\varepsilon$ is strictly greater than
$c$ (as an extended natural number).  This is the easy direction of Yao's minimax principle for
one-way protocols, applied to Index.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Public-coin one-way lower bound at error $1/8$ from the hypothesis]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.div_ten_lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_of_distributionalLowerBound}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.div_ten_lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_of_distributionalLowerBound}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_of_distributionalLowerBound, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.communicationComplexity}
If every deterministic one-way protocol for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ of cost at most
$\lfloor n/10 \rfloor$ has uniform-distributional error greater than $1/8$, then the
public-coin one-way communication complexity of $\mathrm{IND}_n$ at error $1/8$ is strictly
greater than $\lfloor n/10 \rfloor$.  This is the previous theorem specialised to the source's
constants $\varepsilon = 1/8$, $c = \lfloor n/10 \rfloor$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Linear public-coin one-way lower bound for Index]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.div_ten_lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_one_ninth}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.div_ten_lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_one_ninth}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound_one_ninth_of_large, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.lt_publicCoinOneWay_communicationComplexity_of_distributionalLowerBound, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.communicationComplexity}
For $n \ge 300$, the public-coin one-way communication complexity of $\mathrm{IND}_n$ at error
$1/9$ is strictly greater than $\lfloor n/10 \rfloor$:
\[
  R^{\to,\mathrm{pub}}_{1/9}(\mathrm{IND}_n) > \lfloor n/10 \rfloor .
\]
This is the Kremer--Nisan--Ron linear lower bound with explicit constants.
\end{theorem}
